nodes.title: 估算局限性与未计入因素
nodes.summary: 当前的 TFP 和 GDP 增长估算是“上限”，因未充分计入企业采用率低、组织调整成本（J 曲线效应）以及难学任务分类的不确定性。实际影响可能显著低于预测值。
paragraphs: 作者明确指出，前述关于 TFP 增长 0.53%-0.66% 及 GDP 增长的估算应被视为上限，实际效果可能更小。主要原因包括三个方面。
首先，企业采用率被高估。数据显示，截至 2019 年，美国仅有不到 1.5% 的企业有 AI 投资，且主要集中在大型制造企业。中小企业采纳速度慢，且若 AI 工具被少数公司垄断，将进一步阻碍普及。
其次，忽略了组织调整成本。重大技术的广泛采用通常伴随漫长的调整期（J 曲线效应），期间生产率可能持平甚至下降。数字技术的历史经验表明，这一平坦期可能长达 20 年，因此未来 10 年的成本节约可能被显著高估。
最后，任务分类存在不确定性。现有的生产率增益证据多来自“易学”任务，而许多实际任务是“难学”的（涉及复杂情境依赖和缺乏明确成功指标），AI 在这些任务上的表现和成本节约能力尚不明确，可能导致整体增益被高估。
此外，估算也未包含 AI 可能产生的“坏任务”（如深度伪造、操纵性广告）对福利的负面影响，这些活动虽计入 GDP，但可能降低社会总福利。

claims.statement: 当前估算忽略了极低的企业 AI 采用率（2019 年<1.5%），特别是中小企业的滞后，这可能导致 GDP 影响被高估。

Finally, I note three important considerations missing from these computations.


   1. These adoption numbers ignore the fact that there is still very little investment in AI

      in the US corporate sector. Acemoglu et al. (2022) estimate that less than 1.5% of

    US businesses had any investment in AI in 2019, and this is particularly true beyond

     the very large companies in manufacturing, information services and business services.

     Since many of the tasks considered in Eloundou et al. (2023) are performed in small

     and medium-sized enterprises, this is unlikely to change quickly.   If generative AI

      tools become monopolized in the hands of a few companies, this might further slow

    down their adoption by small and medium-sized firms. These considerations suggest

     that even the 0.046% number for the share of GDP impacted by AI may be a big

      overestimate, and the true numbers could be much smaller.

   2. Any major technology creates adjustment costs when adopted at large scale, because

     other organizational aspects need to evolve as well and this is typically quite costly

     and slow. In the context of digital technologies, Greenwood and Yorukoglu (1997) and

      Brynjolfsson et al. (2021), among others, have argued that productivity gains will take

     a J-shaped pattern, and the former paper predicts that the flat part of the J-curve lasts

     no less than 20 years for digital technologies.  If so, the 14.4% overall cost reductions

    may be a significant overestimate for the next 10 years.

   3. As already discussed above, some of the tasks in the list of Eloundou et al. (2023) are

      hard-to-learn, where productivity gains may be significantly less than those based on

     the experimental studies that have focused on the easy-to-learn tasks.


   In the next subsection, I make a preliminary attempt at incorporating the third possi-

bility, but I will ignore the first two. Nevertheless, these considerations make me conclude

that even the 0.66% increase in TFP within the next 10 years due to AI is likely to be an

upper bound on this technology’s medium-run effects.

   In this paper, I use the task-based framework of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018, 2019b,

2022) to evaluate the second and the third effects, and I also take some steps to formalize

how the fourth set of effects might work out in a task-based macro framework.

    I base my approach on existing experimental studies that estimate productivity gains and

time savings from the use of generative AI tools in a number of settings. By building on these

studies, I am explicitly taking on board the idea that generative AI will lead to productivity

improvements. Nevertheless, combining these numbers with estimates of exposed tasks from

Eloundou et al. (2023) and Svanberg et al. (2024) leads to much more modest productivity

effects than most commentators and economists have claimed so far. These numbers become

even smaller once we take into account that many of the tasks for which we have evidence of

cost savings are relatively easy for AI, while in several other tasks the integration of AI will

face more formidable difficulties—mostly because these are likely to involve more complex

interactions between action and context and because they lack clear metrics for success that

are observable, and hence necessitate AI models to learn from the (average) behavior of

humans previously performing the same tasks.

   Taking these considerations into account, I estimate that TFP effects from AI advances

within the next 10 years will be modest—an upper bound that does not take into account

the distinction between hard and easy tasks would be about a 0.66% increase in total within

10 years, or about a 0.064% increase in annual TFP growth. When the presence of hard

tasks among those that will be exposed to AI is recognized, this upper bound drops to

about 0.53%. GDP effects will be somewhat larger than this because automation and task

complementarities will also lead to greater investment. But my calculations suggest that the

GDP boost within the next 10 years should also be modest, in the range of 0.93% −1.16%

over 10 years in total, provided that the investment increase resulting from AI is modest,

and in the range of 1.4% −1.56% in total, if there is a large investment boom.

     If AI is used to create new tasks and products, these will also add to GDP and can

boost productivity growth.  Nevertheless, when we incorporate the possibility that new

tasks generated by AI may be manipulative, the impact on welfare can be even smaller.

Based on numbers from Bursztyn et al. (2023), which pertain to the negative effects of AI-

powered social media, I provide an illustrative calculation for social media, digital ads and

IT defense-attack spending. These could add to GDP by as much as 2%, but if we apply

the numbers from Bursztyn et al. (2023), their impact on welfare may be −0.72%. This

discussion suggests that it is important to consider the potential negative implications of

AI-generated new tasks and products on welfare.

    Finally, I borrow heavily from the estimates of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2022) on the

economy-wide productivity, wage and inequality effects of pre-AI automation technologies

to provide some guidance on what the impact of new AI advances will be.  Because AI-

exposed tasks are more equally distributed within the population than tasks exposed to

pre-AI automation, I do not find substantial negative wage effects for any education group.

Nevertheless, the estimates do not point to significant reductions in inequality either, and

in fact, my findings suggest that low-education women may experience small wage declines,

overall between-group inequality may increase slightly, and the gap between capital and

labor income is likely to widen further.

   These results should not be interpreted as arguing that there are no major benefits from

AI. First, an increase of about 0.53 −0.66% in TFP within 10 years is modest but still far

from trivial. Second and more importantly, there may be other ways in which AI can be used

to generate much more notable benefits. I have suggested in previous work (Acemoglu, 2021,

Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020b) that if AI is used for generating new tasks for workers, it can

have more beneficial productivity, wage and inequality consequences, and it can even increase

wages. This may be doubly true for generative AI, which could be used for providing better

information to workers and boosting their expertise, as argued in Acemoglu et al. (2023)

and explained briefly here.

  Many production workers today, including electricians, repair workers, plumbers, nurses,

educators, clerical workers, and increasingly many blue-collar workers in factories, are en-

gaged in problem-solving tasks. These tasks require real-time, context-dependent and reli-

able information. For instance, an electrician dealing with the malfunctioning of advanced

equipment or a short-circuit on the electricity grid will be hampered from solving these prob-

lems because he or she does not have sufficient expertise and the appropriate information

for troubleshooting.  Reliable information that can be provided quickly by generative AI

tools can lead to significant improvements in productivity. Similarly, generative AI in class-

S009.quote:
This paper evaluates claims about large macroeconomic implications of new advances in AI. It starts
from a task-based model of AI’s effects, working through automation and task complementarities. So long
as AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings/productivity improvements at the task level, its
macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: GDP and aggregate productivity
gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings. Using
existing estimates on exposure to AI and productivity improvements at the task level, these macroeconomic
effects appear nontrivial but modest—no more than a 0.66% increase in total factor productivity (TFP) over
10 years. The paper then argues that even these estimates could be exaggerated, because early evidence
is from easy-to-learn tasks, whereas some of the future effects will come from hard-to-learn tasks, where
there are many context-dependent factors affecting decision-making and no objective outcome measures
from which to learn successful performance. Consequently, predicted TFP gains over the next 10 years
are even more modest and are predicted to be less than 0.53%. I also explore AI’s wage and inequality
effects. I show theoretically that even when AI improves the productivity of low-skill workers in certain
tasks (without creating new tasks for them), this may increase rather than reduce inequality. Empirically,
I find that AI advances are unlikely to increase inequality as much as previous automation technologies
because their impact is more equally distributed across demographic groups, but there is also no evidence
that AI will reduce labor income inequality. Instead, AI is predicted to widen the gap between capital and
labor income. Finally, some of the new tasks created by AI may have negative social value (such as design
of algorithms for online manipulation), and I discuss how to incorporate the macroeconomic effects of new
tasks that may have negative social value.

S013.quote: Artificial intelligence (AI) has captured imaginations. Promises of rapid, even unparalleled,

S014.quote: productivity growth as well as new pathways for complementing humans have become com-

S015.quote: monplace. There is no doubt that recent developments in generative AI and large language

S016.quote: models that produce text, information and images—and Shakespearean sonnets—in response

S017.quote: to simple user prompts are impressive and even spellbinding. ChatGPT, originally released

S018.quote: on November 30, 2022, soon became the fastest spreading tech platform in history, with an

S019.quote: estimated 100 million monthly users only two months after launch.

S020.quote: AI will have implications for the macroeconomy, productivity, wages and inequality, but

S021.quote: all of them are very hard to predict. This has not stopped a series of forecasts over the last

S022.quote: year, often centering on the productivity gains that AI will trigger. Some experts believe

S023.quote: that truly transformative implications, including artificial general intelligence (AGI) enabling

S024.quote: AI to perform essentially all human tasks, could be around the corner.1 Other forecasters

S025.quote: are more grounded, but still predict big effects on output. Goldman Sachs (2023) predicts

S026.quote: a 7% increase in global GDP, equivalent to $7 trillion, and a 1.5% per annum increase in

S027.quote: US productivity growth over a 10-year period. Recent McKinsey Global Institute (2023)

S028.quote: forecasts suggest that generative AI could offer a boost as large as $17.1 to $25.6 trillion to

S029.quote: the global economy, on top of the earlier estimates of economic growth from increased work

S030.quote: automation. They reckon that the overall impact of AI and other automation technologies

S031.quote: could produce up to a 1.5 −3.4 percentage point rise in average annual GDP growth in

S032.quote: advanced economies over the coming decade.2

S1003.quote: by Bresnahan (2019) and Agrawal et al. (2023). It is even more challenging to put numbers

S1004.quote: on the effects of new tasks. If AI helps create new tasks that increase productivity and espe-

S1005.quote: cially contributes to the reinstatement of workers of different skill levels into the production

S1006.quote: process, its consequences can be much more positive.

S1007.quote: Here my purpose is simply to point out that in the case of AI, because some of the new

S1008.quote: tasks may be of the “bad” type, there may be an overstatement of the welfare gains from

S1009.quote: AI when we look at GDP numbers. As an extremely preliminary attempt to argue that this

S1010.quote: could be important, I will draw on two sources of data.

S1011.quote: The first is the recent study by Bursztyn et al. (2023), which provides suggestive esti-

S1012.quote: mates for the extent of this problem in the case of social media. Bursztyn et al. (2023) run

S1013.quote: an experiment to evaluate the welfare effects of social media for college students, the demo-

S1014.quote: graphic group most engaged with social media. They ask TikTok and Instagram users how

S1015.quote: much they would need to be paid to not use the platform for a month. Users of these two

S1016.quote: platforms are willing to pay up to $59 and $47 a month, respectively, to continue to use social

S1017.quote: media—or on average $53 per user-month. However, they find that users are also willing

S1018.quote: to pay $28 and $10 every month to get everyone from their social network off TikTok and

S1019.quote: Instagram, respectively—or an average $19 per user-month. If non-users are also included in

S1020.quote: the analysis, the willingness to pay to stop everybody using social media increases to $47 for

S1021.quote: TikTok and $13 for Instagram. This suggests that while companies can profitably market

S1022.quote: AI-based social media, the net effect on welfare may be negative. Quantitatively, I ignore

S1023.quote: the non-users (since the population in the study is college students, who are more likely to be

S1024.quote: impacted by social media activity even when they do not use it than the adult population in

S1025.quote: the United States). I also start with a benchmark in which AI-powered platforms can capture

S1026.quote: the full (average) $53 willingness to pay per user (for example, because they are effectively

S1027.quote: price discriminating by varying the intensity with which they are collecting and monetizing

S1028.quote: users’ data). Then taking the average between the two platforms, I conclude that for every

S1029.quote: $53 of revenue, there is a net negative effect on users of $19. Put differently, the total effect

S1030.quote: from this class of new bad tasks, the equivalent of (18) in theory, is −19/53 ≃−0.36 in

S1031.quote: proportionate terms. Note also that if I assumed instead that social media companies can

S1032.quote: capture less than the full $53 per user-month, then the denominator in this expression would

S1033.quote: be smaller, and thus the proportionate damage per dollar of revenue would be higher.

S1034.quote: I combine the number −0.36 with estimates of (i) revenues from social media and digital

S1035.quote: ads, and (ii) spending on malicious IT attacks and IT security against these attacks to

S1036.quote: compute apparent and real gains from new bad tasks. Specifically, the total revenues in 2022

S1037.quote: of Meta (Facebook plus Instagram), Alphabet (Google and Youtube), Snapchat, TikTok and

S1038.quote: Twitter (“X”) comes to 460 billion, or about 1.64% of US GDP,28 while a lower bound on IT

S1039.quote: security is 78 billion or 0.28% of US GDP.29 Assuming that spending by malicious actors on

S1040.quote: IT attacks is at least one third of this and combining these three estimates, I arrive to 2% of

S1041.quote: US GDP. This number could be a significant underestimate of other manipulative activities

S1042.quote: enabled by new AI technologies. On the other hand, it could also overstate the problem, since

S1043.quote: only a fraction of digital ad revenues will come from such manipulative activities (and this

S1044.quote: may be particularly true for digital ad revenues from Google search). These considerations

S1045.quote: suggest that the numbers here should be taken as merely suggestive.

S1046.quote: Taking the 2% of US GDP as revenues from new bad tasks and using the numbers from

S1047.quote: Bursztyn et al. (2023) suggests that the total negative effects of these manipulative activities

S1048.quote: is 0.02 × 0.36 = 0.072% of GDP (in consumption equivalent units). This number points to a

S1049.quote: sizable negative impact on welfare, and could be larger if manipulative uses of generative AI

S1050.quote: becomes more widespread. In contrast, if one were to simply count the revenue coming from

S1051.quote: these new tasks, one might conclude that they would increase GDP by 2%. This discussion

S1052.quote: thus suggests caution in interpreting all increases in GDP coming from the use of generative

S1053.quote: AI as a positive effect on consumer welfare.

S1226.quote: Following its release on November 30, 2022, ChatGPT became the fastest spreading tech plat-

S1227.quote: form in history, reaching approximately 100 million monthly users within just two months.

S1228.quote: Its impressive features, and the greater capabilities of the newer version ChatGPT-4, released

S1229.quote: in March 2023, soon captured imaginations, both among the general public and economic

S1230.quote: commentators. Forecasts of large productivity gains have now become commonplace.

S1231.quote: While there is no question that generative AI models, including ChatGPT, have impres-

S1232.quote: sive achievements and have great potential for beneficial economic effects, the extent of their

S1233.quote: macroeconomic consequences remains an open question.

S1250.quote: In this paper, I use the task-based framework of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018, 2019b,

S1251.quote: 2022) to evaluate the second and the third effects, and I also take some steps to formalize

S1252.quote: how the fourth set of effects might work out in a task-based macro framework.

S1253.quote: I base my approach on existing experimental studies that estimate productivity gains and

S1254.quote: time savings from the use of generative AI tools in a number of settings. By building on these

S1255.quote: studies, I am explicitly taking on board the idea that generative AI will lead to productivity

S1256.quote: improvements. Nevertheless, combining these numbers with estimates of exposed tasks from

S1257.quote: Eloundou et al. (2023) and Svanberg et al. (2024) leads to much more modest productivity

S1258.quote: effects than most commentators and economists have claimed so far. These numbers become

S1259.quote: even smaller once we take into account that many of the tasks for which we have evidence of

S1260.quote: cost savings are relatively easy for AI, while in several other tasks the integration of AI will

S1261.quote: face more formidable difficulties—mostly because these are likely to involve more complex

S1262.quote: interactions between action and context and because they lack clear metrics for success that

S1263.quote: are observable, and hence necessitate AI models to learn from the (average) behavior of

S1264.quote: humans previously performing the same tasks.

S1265.quote: Taking these considerations into account, I estimate that TFP effects from AI advances

S1266.quote: within the next 10 years will be modest—an upper bound that does not take into account

S1267.quote: the distinction between hard and easy tasks would be about a 0.66% increase in total within

S1268.quote: 10 years, or about a 0.064% increase in annual TFP growth. When the presence of hard

S1269.quote: tasks among those that will be exposed to AI is recognized, this upper bound drops to

S1270.quote: about 0.53%. GDP effects will be somewhat larger than this because automation and task

S1271.quote: complementarities will also lead to greater investment. But my calculations suggest that the

S1272.quote: GDP boost within the next 10 years should also be modest, in the range of 0.93% −1.16%

S1273.quote: over 10 years in total, provided that the investment increase resulting from AI is modest,

S1274.quote: and in the range of 1.4% −1.56% in total, if there is a large investment boom.

S1275.quote: If AI is used to create new tasks and products, these will also add to GDP and can

S1276.quote:
boost productivity growth.
Nevertheless, when we incorporate the possibility that new

S1277.quote: tasks generated by AI may be manipulative, the impact on welfare can be even smaller.

S1278.quote: Based on numbers from Bursztyn et al. (2023), which pertain to the negative effects of AI-

S1279.quote: powered social media, I provide an illustrative calculation for social media, digital ads and

S1280.quote: IT defense-attack spending. These could add to GDP by as much as 2%, but if we apply

S1281.quote: the numbers from Bursztyn et al. (2023), their impact on welfare may be −0.72%. This

S1282.quote: discussion suggests that it is important to consider the potential negative implications of

S1284.quote: Finally, I borrow heavily from the estimates of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2022) on the

S1285.quote: economy-wide productivity, wage and inequality effects of pre-AI automation technologies

S1286.quote: to provide some guidance on what the impact of new AI advances will be. Because AI-

S1287.quote: exposed tasks are more equally distributed within the population than tasks exposed to

S1288.quote: pre-AI automation, I do not find substantial negative wage effects for any education group.

S1289.quote: Nevertheless, the estimates do not point to significant reductions in inequality either, and

S1290.quote: in fact, my findings suggest that low-education women may experience small wage declines,

S1291.quote: overall between-group inequality may increase slightly, and the gap between capital and

S1292.quote: labor income is likely to widen further.

S1296.quote: to generate much more notable benefits. I have suggested in previous work (Acemoglu, 2021,

S1297.quote: Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020b) that if AI is used for generating new tasks for workers, it can

S1298.quote: have more beneficial productivity, wage and inequality consequences, and it can even increase

S1302.quote: Many production workers today, including electricians, repair workers, plumbers, nurses,

S1303.quote: educators, clerical workers, and increasingly many blue-collar workers in factories, are en-

S1304.quote: gaged in problem-solving tasks. These tasks require real-time, context-dependent and reli-

S1305.quote: able information. For instance, an electrician dealing with the malfunctioning of advanced

S1306.quote: equipment or a short-circuit on the electricity grid will be hampered from solving these prob-

S1307.quote: lems because he or she does not have sufficient expertise and the appropriate information

S1308.quote: for troubleshooting. Reliable information that can be provided quickly by generative AI

S1309.quote: tools can lead to significant improvements in productivity. Similarly, generative AI in class-

S1310.quote: rooms can lead to a major reorganization of how teaching takes place, with greater levels

S1311.quote: of personalization, as these tools help teachers identify specific aspects of the curriculum

S1312.quote: with which subgroups of students are having problems and propose new context-dependent

S1313.quote: teaching strategies. Reliability of AI models will be key for successfully creating such new

S1314.quote: tasks and delivering improvements in the quality of education.

S1315.quote: Productivity improvements from new tasks and new products, which have been impor-

S1316.quote: tant for previous transformative technologies, such as electricity and the Internet, are not

S1320.quote: not to include these in the likely macroeconomic effects, because these are not the areas

S1321.quote: receiving attention from the industry at the moment, as also argued in Acemoglu (2021),

S1322.quote: Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020b) and Acemoglu and Johnson (2023). Rather, areas of pri-

S1323.quote: ority for the tech industry appear to be around automation and monetization of personal

S1324.quote: data, such as through search or social media digital ads. This makes it less likely that many

S1325.quote: new good tasks will be created quickly.Third, and relatedly, more beneficial outcomes may

S1326.quote: require new institutions, policies and regulations, as also suggested in Acemoglu and Johnson

S1328.quote: My assessment is that there are indeed much bigger gains to be had from generative AI,

S1329.quote: which is a promising technology, but these gains will remain elusive unless there is a funda-

S1330.quote: mental reorientation of the industry, including perhaps a major change in the architecture

S1331.quote: of the most common generative AI models, such as the LLMs, in order to focus on reliable

S1332.quote: information that can increase the marginal productivity of different kinds of workers, rather

S1333.quote: than prioritizing the development of general human-like conversational tools. The general-

S1334.quote: purpose nature of the current approach to generative AI could be ill-suited for providing

S1335.quote: such reliable information. To put it simply, it remains an open question whether we need

S1336.quote: foundation models (or the current kind of LLMs) that can engage in human-like conver-

S1337.quote: sations and write Shakespearean sonnets if what we want is reliable information useful for

S1338.quote: educators, healthcare professionals, electricians, plumbers and other craft workers.

S1495.quote: The procedure used for classifying “easy-to-learn” (or “easy”) and “hard-to-learn” (or

S1496.quote: “hard”) tasks is described at a high level in the text. Here I provide further details.

S1497.quote: We start with Eloundou et al’s exposure measure and focus on three features of tasks (i)

S1498.quote: primary verbs, (ii) IWAs, and (iii) topic clusters coded by LDA.

S1499.quote: 1. Primary verbs: Each task on O*NET has a task description that starts with at

S1500.quote: least one verb. These “primary” verbs are informative about what the task involves

S1501.quote: and how easily a task can be automated using AI. In particular, verbs that indicate

S1502.quote: objective measurement possibilities for the outcome (e.g., calculate or quantify) or

S1503.quote: involve predictable rules that allow for easy mapping to outcomes (estimate) are more

S1504.quote: likely to be associated with easy tasks.

S1505.quote: We manually classified verbs as easy, hard or uncertain, where the last category con-

S1506.quote: tains verbs that are harder to classify or involve both harder and easier elements (for

S1507.quote: which the context will be important as I describe next). The full list of verbs and their

S1508.quote: classifications are provided in the replication package, and the most common hard and

S1509.quote: easy verbs are listed in Table A-1 in this Appendix.

S1510.quote: 2. Intermediate Work Activities: Each task on O*NET is situated within a hierarchy

S1511.quote: and is associated with at least one Detailed Work Activity (DWA), which is a coarser

S1512.quote: description of the task. Each DWA is in turn associated with at least one Intermediate

S1513.quote: Work Activity (IWA), which is at a higher level aggregation. There are 19264 tasks

S1514.quote: and 332 IWAs in O*NET. While verbs are informative on whether the observed act is

S1515.quote: associated with a predictable outcome, IWAs provide context about the observability of

S1516.quote: the outcome. For example, explaining can be hard-to-learn when it is in the context of

S1517.quote: teaching key concepts to elementary school students, but easy-to-learn when it involves

S1518.quote: explaining the rules of a parlor game. We manually classified each IWA as easy or hard

S1519.quote: taking this context into account. The replication package also includes the exact list

S1521.quote: 3. Topic clusters: We use a separate unsupervised learning algorithm, the Latent Dirich-

S1522.quote: let Allocation (LDA) algorithm (Blei et al., 2003), to determine probabilistic topic

S1523.quote: clusters. Topic clusters provide an additional layer of context for the algorithm. We

S1524.quote: apply the LDA algorithm to all 19264 tasks to generate 100 topic clusters. LDA lever-

S1525.quote: ages word co-occurence within task statements to determine probabilistic assignment

S1526.quote: of each task to topic clusters.

S1527.quote: We use the output of these three steps with our supervised learning model, which is a

S1528.quote: gradient boosted classifier (GBC) (Friedman, 2001). GBCs maximize goodness-of-fit over a

S1529.quote: training set by iteratively generating partitions. We produce the training set by manually

S1530.quote: classifying 757 of the 4089 exposed tasks. The GBC produces the best fit for these 757 tasks,

S1531.quote: and we obtain the output of the classifier for the remaining tasks. The inputs into the GBC

S1532.quote: are: the verb classification, the IWA classification, and probabilities to belonging to each

S1533.quote: one of the 100 topic clusters from the LDA. In addition, we also feed the GBC the empirical

S1534.quote: frequencies of each verb being associated with an easy or uncertain task (hard task being the

S1535.quote: omitted category), and each IWA being associated with an easy task in our training data.

S1536.quote: This information is useful as it provides an empirical measure of the degree of certainty with

S1537.quote: which each verb and IWA is classified (analogous to the prior in a Bayesian calculation).

S1538.quote: When a task has more than one primary verb, we take the average across these.

近日，学院2022级本科生周祺在电力学院戴栋教授的指导下，作为共同第一作者，在国际学术期刊《Nature Machine Intelligence》发表研究论文，这是学院本科生首次以第一作者身份在Nature子刊上发表论文。
该研究提出了“自由边界神经算子（FBNO）”通用框架，首次将神经算子方法的适用边界从预先给定的固定区域拓展至先验未知、动态演化的复杂区域填补了神经算子框架长期以来无法直接求解自由边界问题（FBPs）的研究空白。
自由边界问题（Free Boundary Problems, FBPs）广泛存在于相变物理、肿瘤生长仿真、等离子体动力学、生物力学及连续介质力学等诸多前沿理工学科，是多领域共性关键科学问题。该类问题存在两大核心技术瓶颈：一方面，模型求解区域具备强时间动态演化特性，边界几何形态无法提前先验获知；另一方面，全域物理场分布与区域几何边界存在强双向耦合关系，二者相互制约、协同演化，进一步提升了数值求解难度。
现有主流求解手段均存在难以规避的局限性：传统数值求解方案依托动网格更新、求解域动态重构等策略适配边界变化，整体计算流程复杂、算力开销比较大，难以满足参数搜索或是物理场优化等大规模仿真需求。近年来，快速发展的神经算子方法在固定求解域偏微分方程（PDE）求解任务中，已实现最高五个数量级的运算加速，具备优异的高效求解优势，但该类方法存在本质性约束，即必须依托预先确定的固定函数定义域开展建模与计算，无法适配动态变化的未知求解域，故而无法直接应用于自由边界问题求解。

concept-68d1f51a03d453e7.lead: 连接微观生产力冲击与宏观总生产力增长的桥梁。
concept-68d1f51a03d453e7.text: 在竞争性经济且规模报酬不变的假设下，总要素生产率（TFP）的增长率等于各部门（或任务）生产率增长率的加权平均，权重为该部门（或任务）在总产出中的份额。这意味着微小的微观效率提升，若发生在产出份额大的领域，将对宏观经济产生显著影响；反之则影响有限。
concept-68d1f51a03d453e7.why: 理解此概念至关重要，因为它是本文推导 AI 宏观影响上限的理论基石，解释了为何即使某些任务效率大幅提升，若其经济份额小，整体 GDP 增长依然有限。

concept-a1e92b804f8570d4.title: 任务互补性 (Task Complementarities)
concept-a1e92b804f8570d4.lead: AI 不仅替代人类劳动，还能增强人类在特定任务中的生产力。
concept-a1e92b804f8570d4.text: 指 AI 技术与人类劳动结合，使得人类在执行某些任务时效率更高，而非完全取代人类。在这种模式下，AI 的作用是降低完成任务的总成本或提高产出质量，从而产生成本节约效应。本文指出，Hulten 定理同样适用于由互补性带来的生产力提升。
concept-a1e92b804f8570d4.why: 区分自动化与互补性有助于全面理解 AI 的影响机制。本文强调无论哪种机制，只要产生成本节约，都纳入同一宏观框架计算。

concept-9acd4a53e28a801e.title: 全要素生产率 (Total Factor Productivity, TFP)
concept-9acd4a53e28a801e.lead: 衡量除资本和劳动投入外，由技术进步和效率提升带来的产出增长。
concept-9acd4a53e28a801e.text: TFP 是产出增长中不能由资本或劳动投入增加解释的部分，通常被视为技术进步的代理指标。在本文中，AI 带来的成本节约被视为一种技术进步，直接体现为 TFP 的增长。作者计算的 0.66% 是指 10 年累计的 TFP 水平提升，而非年增长率。
concept-9acd4a53e28a801e.why: 这是本文评估 AI 经济价值的核心指标。理解 TFP 有助于区分由单纯增加资源投入带来的增长与由效率提升带来的真实经济增长。

concept-828b5975ee803f3b.title: 工资单份额 (Wage Bill Share)
concept-828b5975ee803f3b.lead: 用于加权不同职业在经济中的重要程度。
concept-828b5975ee803f3b.text: 指某一职业或行业的工资总额占整个经济体工资总额的比例。作者在计算受 AI 影响的任务比例时，没有简单地对任务数量求平均，而是使用工资单份额作为权重。这意味着高薪资、大规模的职业（如软件开发、管理）对结果的影响更大，更能反映 AI 对整体经济的实际冲击。
concept-828b5975ee803f3b.why: 使用工资单份额加权能更准确地反映 AI 对宏观经济总量（如 GDP）的潜在影响，避免了低薪或小众任务对估算结果的过度干扰。

concept-c7e7cf727af2c237.title: 客观结果指标 (Objective Outcome Metric)
concept-c7e7cf727af2c237.lead: 衡量任务是否成功完成的明确、可量化的标准。
concept-c7e7cf727af2c237.text: 指在任务执行过程中，能够清晰判断结果好坏的标准（例如：代码是否编译通过、图像分类是否正确、鸡蛋是否达到指定熟度）。易学任务通常具备此类指标，使得监督学习算法能够有效优化。难学任务往往缺乏此类指标，或者指标极其复杂、多维，导致 AI 难以通过常规训练获得高性能。
concept-c7e7cf727af2c237.why: 这是区分易学与难学任务的核心标准之一。缺乏客观指标意味着 AI 无法通过最小化损失函数来明确改进方向，从而限制了其在复杂决策任务中的应用效果。

concept-f4b3b7565f6e66bb.title: 情境依赖型决策 (Context-Dependent Decision)
concept-f4b3b7565f6e66bb.lead: 决策结果高度依赖于特定环境因素，难以通过通用规则概括。
concept-f4b3b7565f6e66bb.text: 指在任务执行中，最佳行动方案随具体情境（如患者病史、市场情绪、人际互动细节）的变化而剧烈变化，不存在单一的、低维的规则可以涵盖所有情况。这类任务通常需要人类专家的直觉、经验和判断力，AI 难以仅凭历史数据捕捉所有相关的情境变量，因此在这些领域的表现提升有限。
concept-f4b3b7565f6e66bb.why: 解释了为何 AI 在某些看似简单的任务上表现优异，而在涉及复杂人类互动的任务上却显得笨拙。这是难学任务生产力增益受限的根本原因。

concept-127ae0e2a8218851.title: 全要素生产率 (TFP)
concept-127ae0e2a8218851.lead: 衡量技术进步对产出的贡献
concept-127ae0e2a8218851.text: 全要素生产率（Total Factor Productivity, TFP）是指在扣除资本和劳动投入增长后，剩余的经济产出增长部分，通常被视为技术进步的代理指标。在本文中，AI 通过降低任务成本来提升 TFP。
concept-127ae0e2a8218851.why: 理解 TFP 是评估 AI 宏观经济影响的核心，因为 GDP 增长在很大程度上取决于 TFP 的提升幅度。

concept-de4d6b315df9227a.title: Hulten 定理
concept-de4d6b315df9227a.lead: 连接微观生产力与宏观 GDP 的桥梁
concept-de4d6b315df9227a.text: Hulten 定理指出，在一般均衡条件下， aggregate productivity (TFP) 的增长可以近似为各 sector/task 生产力加权的总和。本文利用该定理，将任务层面的成本节约汇总为宏观层面的 TFP 和 GDP 增长估算。
concept-de4d6b315df9227a.why: 该定理是作者从微观任务数据推导宏观经济增长预测的理论基础。

concept-07f80557bcf17295.title: 负外部性 (Negative Externality)
concept-07f80557bcf17295.lead: 未被市场价格反映的社会成本
concept-07f80557bcf17295.text: 负外部性指经济活动对第三方产生的未补偿的负面影响。在本文中，AI 驱动的操纵性广告或深度伪造虽然产生企业收入（计入 GDP），但对用户造成心理或社会损害，这种损害未体现在市场价格中，构成负外部性。
concept-07f80557bcf17295.why: 这是解释为何 GDP 增长不一定代表福利增加的关键概念，也是作者构建 W = C - E 福利函数的基础。

concept-3bc99a230d84653b.title: 涟漪效应 (Ripple Effect)
concept-3bc99a230d84653b.lead: 劳动力市场冲击的间接传播
concept-3bc99a230d84653b.text: 涟漪效应指某一 demographic group 受到技术冲击（如自动化）后，被迫与其他群体竞争原本由后者占据的任务，从而将负面影响传导至其他群体。在本文中，低技能工人可能因 AI 而被挤出原有任务，进而加剧内部竞争或影响其他低技能组别。
concept-3bc99a230d84653b.why: 这是解释为何局部生产力提升可能导致整体不平等恶化的重要机制，特别是在多技能组别的复杂模型中。

concept-eb4e6a458ed0aa93.title: 涟漪效应 (Ripple Effects)
concept-eb4e6a458ed0aa93.lead: 指技术冲击通过行业间投入产出关联和要素流动，间接影响非直接暴露群体的工资和就业。
concept-eb4e6a458ed0aa93.text: 在本文框架中，涟漪效应是指 AI 对某些行业或任务的直接冲击（如成本降低或劳动力需求减少），通过改变相对价格和要素需求，进而波及其他行业或 demographic groups 的间接影响。作者发现，由于 AI 的直接暴露分布较为均匀，涟漪效应并未显著改变不平等的总体格局。
concept-eb4e6a458ed0aa93.why: 理解涟漪效应有助于解释为何直接暴露度均匀的 AI 技术仍可能通过一般均衡机制对整体工资结构产生复杂影响，是评估技术宏观后果的关键环节。

concept-f5e756b628637270.title: 资本份额 (Capital Share)
concept-f5e756b628637270.lead: 国民收入中归属于资本所有者的比例，通常与劳动份额相对。
concept-f5e756b628637270.text: 在宏观经济学中，资本份额指总产出或总收入中支付给资本（如利润、利息、租金）的部分。本文预测，由于 AI 提高了资本的生产效率或替代了部分劳动，资本份额将上升，这意味着国民收入分配将更有利于资本所有者，从而扩大资本与劳动之间的收入差距。
concept-f5e756b628637270.why: 资本份额的变化是衡量技术进步对收入分配影响的核心指标之一，直接关系到不平等趋势的判断。

concept-e458a8d00644337f.title: TFP 到 GDP 的转化 (TFP to GDP Conversion)
concept-e458a8d00644337f.lead: 将全要素生产率的增长转化为国内生产总值增长的过程，需考虑要素投入（特别是资本）的调整。
concept-e458a8d00644337f.text: 在增长核算框架下，GDP 的增长不仅来源于 TFP 的提高，还来源于资本和劳动投入的增加。当 TFP 提高时，资本的边际产出增加，通常会诱导投资增加，从而进一步放大 GDP 的增长。本文展示了如何在不同投资响应假设下进行这种转化计算。
concept-e458a8d00644337f.why: 这是理解技术进步如何转化为宏观经济总量指标的关键步骤，忽略了资本响应会低估 GDP 潜力，但过度强调投资也可能误导福利判断。

concept-5fbd61b5acae701e.title: 资本深化 (Capital Deepening)
concept-5fbd61b5acae701e.lead: 指人均资本存量的增加，通常由技术进步诱导投资所致。
concept-5fbd61b5acae701e.text: 资本深化是指每个工人拥有的资本量增加的过程。在本文语境下，若 AI 引发强烈的投资响应，导致资本存量增长速度超过 TFP 增长速度，即发生资本深化。虽然这会推高 GDP，但若投资资金来源于减少当前消费，则不一定提高长期福利。
concept-5fbd61b5acae701e.why: 区分 TFP 驱动的增长和资本深化驱动的增长对于评估技术的真实福利效应至关重要。

concept-8004e6e6ddf4e6e1.title: J 曲线效应 (J-Curve Effect)
concept-8004e6e6ddf4e6e1.lead: 指新技术引入初期，由于学习成本和重组摩擦，生产率暂时停滞或下降，随后才显著上升的现象。
concept-8004e6e6ddf4e6e1.text: 在技术扩散文献中，J 曲线效应描述了新通用技术（如电力、计算机、AI）被广泛采用时的典型路径：初期企业需投入资源进行组织重构和员工培训，导致短期生产率未见提升甚至下降；只有经过较长的磨合期后，生产率才会大幅跃升。本文引用此概念警示 AI 的短期宏观收益可能被高估。
concept-8004e6e6ddf4e6e1.why: 理解 J 曲线效应有助于设定合理的时间预期，避免将长期的潜在收益错误地投射到短期（如未来 10 年）预测中。

concept-f5f997abac4f1d78.title: 易学与难学任务 (Easy-to-Learn vs. Hard-to-Learn Tasks)
concept-f5f997abac4f1d78.lead: 根据 AI 模型能否从现有数据中有效学习并达到高性能，将任务分为两类。
concept-f5f997abac4f1d78.text: 易学任务通常有明确的输入输出映射和客观的成功指标，AI 能通过监督学习快速掌握并超越人类表现。难学任务则涉及高度情境依赖的决策、缺乏清晰的反馈信号或需要复杂的常识推理，目前 AI 在这些任务上的表现受限且成本节约不确定。本文强调现有实验多基于易学任务，因此外推到整体经济时需谨慎。
concept-f5f997abac4f1d78.why: 这一区分是修正 TFP 增长估计的关键，解释了为何基于早期实验数据的乐观预测可能在宏观层面失效。
